rationale: Multiple independent clinical and genetic reports confirm that heterozygous loss-of-function alleles in SPTAN1 (including nonsense mutations and 9q34 microdeletions) exhibit incomplete/reduced penetrance alongside marked clinical variability. Notably, Van de Vondel et al. (2026) documented a 9q34 microdeletion encompassing SPTAN1 segregating in four affected individuals while remaining non-penetrant in two verified carrier relatives (2/6, or 33.3% non-penetrance). Earlier founding work by Beijer et al. (2019) demonstrated reduced penetrance with asymptomatic or subclinical carriers across two of three autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuropathy kindreds, corroborated further by Dong et al. (2021) and international diagnostic curation panels (Genomics England and Australian PanelApp). No reports contradict the existence of reduced penetrance or demonstrate mandatory 100% penetrance for SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants.

evidence.text: A heterozygous 9q34 microdeletion encompassing SPTAN1 segregated in four clinically affected patients presenting with childhood-onset distal muscle weakness and was explicitly non-penetrant in two other carrier relatives.

new_directions.question_text: What genetic or epigenetic modifiers compensate for SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency to prevent disease expression in asymptomatic carriers?
new_directions.rationale: Fibroblast and tissue assays show reduced transcript levels via nonsense-mediated decay without commensurate total loss of alpha-II-spectrin protein in some non-penetrant carriers, indicating active translational or post-translational compensatory pathways.

new_directions.question_text: Does subclinical axonal motor loss or subclinical myopathic change exist on quantitative electrophysiology or neuromuscular MRI in asymptomatic heterozygous SPTAN1 carriers?
new_directions.rationale: Determining whether 'non-penetrant' carriers harbor covert denervation/myopathy clarifies whether penetrance is truly incomplete or reflects a mild, subclinical threshold effect.
